newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn to sell oil, meet EMU target - sources.
newsitem.headline: Bonn to sell oil, meet EMU target - sources.

text.p: Germany plans to raise around 400 million marks by selling off oil reserves this year and will meet the deficit target for a single European currency of 3.0 percent of economic output, government sources said on Thursday.

News of the oil sale emerged as members of parliament from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition gave the green light to Finance Minister Theo Waigel's supplementary budget for 1997 and draft budget for 1998.

The supplementary budget for this year, when European Union countries must meet fiscal targets to qualify for the single currency, raises the deficit to 71 billion marks ($40.3 billion), a jump from the originally planned 53.3 billion.
The government's original prediction for this year was a deficit of 2.9 percent. But sources said Bonn would still make the grade for the euro now with a 3.0 percent deficit.

"The supplementary budget is the necessary reaction to a need for increased financing," said Wolfgang Weng, the budget policy spokesman for the liberal Free Democrats, Kohl's junior coalition partners.

Government sources said "positive developments in federal special assets and social security" would help offset the larger federal deficit and meet the deficit target for European monetary union. They gave no further details.

Germany is leaving no stone unturned in its bid to meet the entry criteria for economic and monetary union this year and then stay within those target values, as demanded by the EU's stability pact for the single currency.
Government sources said Germany hoped to raise a total of one billion marks this year and next by disposing of the oil reserves built up after the energy crisis of the 1970s.
Weng said the need for supplementary financing came mainly from higher-than-expected unemployment but he was confident measures taken over the last few years would help the labour market.
"The upturn in the economic situation will make a contribution," he said. "(But) further privatisation and savings measures are needed to improve the budget situation."
Total public sector debt will be slightly over the target of 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the government sources said, but will be brought back into line by 2001.
The 1997 supplementary budget puts the deficit higher than investment -- something the German constitution only allows in the exceptional case of economic imbalance.
Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) budget spokesman Karl Diller attacked Waigel's budget plans, due to be approved by the cabinet on Friday.

"The principle of sustainable security in state finances has been thrown overboard and burdens have just been postponed for the future," Diller said. "Waigel's bridge to 1999 does not rest on a secure bank. It hovers above the abyss."

The government sees growth rates as moderate but steady, the sources said. GDP growth in 1997 is seen at 2.5 percent, rising to 2.75 percent next year and coming back to 2.5 percent in each of the three years following.
In 1998, the deficit is expected to fall back to 57.8 billion marks. Privatisation revenues in 1998 are seen rising to 19.7 billion marks from 12.7 billion this year.
Although the SPD had demanded since February that Waigel present a supplementary budget, Diller said the plan Waigel has come up with did too little to create jobs.

The SPD will oppose the government's plans to cut the solidarity income tax surcharge, raised to help rebuild ex-communist eastern Germany, since they would force states to give up 3.5 billion marks in revenue.
The coalition's tax reform plans, now being debated in parliament's mediation committee, would cut revenues by about 20 billion marks a year, placing additional pressures on the deficit, Diller said.
